DART's performance is further validated through experiments on a range of established bandit problems, demonstrating its superior efficacy compared to other state-of-the-art methods. English as a Second Language (ESL) students are often challenged when learning new vocabulary through reading and writing. To help them develop this skill, ESL teachers commonly use sentence completion exercises, which present students with incomplete sentences containing unknown words and ask them to fill these gaps with the correct word from a given list. Although these exercises are effective, they can be time-consuming and require a significant amount of teacher time to prepare. To address this issue, we have created an AI-powered tool that can help ESL learners practice sentence completion exercises, providing them with a list of words to choose from and an explanation of the correct answer. To make this tool more effective, we have incorporated a feature that uses natural language processing techniques to analyze the context in which the word to be filled is used, providing learners with a better understanding of the word's meaning and its usage. Our tool has been tested with a set of sentence completion exercises, and the results show that it can provide high-quality explanations that are both accurate and informative. In addition, we have conducted a user study to evaluate the effectiveness of our tool in helping ESL learners improve their vocabulary skills, and the results show that it can help learners better understand the words they are learning. Overall, our AI-powered tool has the potential to revolutionize the way ESL learners practice sentence completion exercises, making the process more engaging, efficient, and effective. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that uses natural language processing techniques to provide explanations for sentence completion exercises, and we believe that it has the potential to make a significant impact in the field of ESL education. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AIMAG in detecting and resisting adversarial perturbations in text-to-image synthesis tasks, particularly in image captioning and image retrieval. Our results show that AIMAG can effectively reduce the robustness of state-of-the-art text-to-image synthesis models against adversarial attacks. Link prediction in knowledge graphs has been a major focus area in recent research, 
due to its numerous practical applications. However, existing methods face significant 
challenges in handling missing links within large knowledge graphs, namely the 
scalability issue and the problem of generalizing across diverse knowledge graphs. 
To address these issues, a novel framework called Knowledge Graph Link 
Predictor (KG-OP) has been developed, which leverages the capabilities of 
Optimal Transport (OT) theory to make predictions. By modeling KGs as complex 
dynamics influenced by hidden factors, KG-OP is able to extract meaningful 
patterns from the data, and then utilize OT distance to measure the difference 
between the actual and predicted link structures. The framework's effectiveness 
has been demonstrated through rigorous testing on large-scale datasets, 
demonstrating its ability to outperform current state-of-the-art methods in all 
evaluations. Additionally, KG-OP is shown to be highly adaptable across different 
knowledge graphs, leading to improved generalizability. The source code for KG-OP 
is available for further research and development at the specified repository. 
KG-OP's OT-based approach to link prediction has also been found to be interpretable 
due to the inherent properties of OT distance. The framework's interpretability 
has been demonstrated through a case study on a real-world knowledge graph, 
OpenStreetMap Links of the World (OSMLOW). The framework's source code can be 
accessed at the provided repository.

Transport coefficients for heat and momentum within a Yukawa gas under equilibrium conditions have been derived using statistical mechanics.  An extended version of the Boltzmann equation was utilized to obtain these coefficients, which were specifically calculated for systems consisting of charged particles interacting via a Yukawa potential.  Calculations were made for both neutral and ionized plasmas, with the neutral case being applicable to systems of any mass ratio and the ionized plasma case being applicable to systems of equal mass ratio.  In both scenarios, transport coefficients were expressed in terms of system density and temperature, with the neutral case also being expressed in terms of temperature only.  Additionally, this research included a comparison of the transport coefficients derived using statistical mechanics with those derived using the Chapman-Cowling method.  Notably, while the Chapman-Cowling method is limited to low temperatures and certain mass ratios, the statistical mechanics approach can be applied to a broader range of conditions.  Furthermore, this research demonstrated that the statistical mechanics approach can be applied to any temperature, regardless of the mass ratio, in the case of an ionized plasma.  In the neutral case, this research also included a comparison of the transport coefficients derived using statistical mechanics with those derived using the Enskog equation for hard spheres.  Notably, the Enskog equation is a more accurate representation of the neutral gas at higher densities, with the statistical mechanics approach being applicable to even higher densities.  Finally, this research included a comparison of the transport coefficients derived using statistical mechanics with those derived using the Landau-Lifshitz approximation for the neutral gas at low densities.  Notably, the Landau-Lifshitz approximation is a more accurate representation of the neutral gas at low densities, with the statistical mechanics approach being applicable to even lower densities.  In all cases, the statistical mechanics approach was found to be more accurate than the other methods examined.  This research has provided a comprehensive set of transport coefficients for Yukawa systems of any mass ratio and temperature, which can be applied to a wide range of conditions. Recent advances in unpaired image denoising have been achieved by learning noise patterns from the input image itself. However, this approach is limited by its reliance on the input image's noise characteristics. To overcome this limitation, we propose a structural perspective on unpaired image denoising, where the goal is to identify and replicate the noise patterns found in the target image. By adopting this approach, we can develop a denoising algorithm that is not constrained by the input image's noise statistics. To achieve this, we introduce a two-stage denoising framework, consisting of a structural estimation stage and a structural removal stage. The first stage uses a structural estimation module to identify and replicate the noise patterns found in the target image, while the second stage utilizes a structural removal module to remove the estimated noise, along with a refinement module to fine-tune the results. The proposed method, named Structural Unpaired Denoising (SUD), can effectively remove a wide range of noises and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on various datasets without requiring any training, achieving a substantial improvement of over 10 dB E_NIQE on average. A significant disparity exists in the availability of language resources for Tatar and other minority languages, making it challenging to develop effective NLP applications for these languages. To address this issue, we introduce the Tatar corpus, a newly developed dataset for the Yaul, a Tatar dialect spoken by the Volga and Kama river regions in Russia. The Yaul corpus is unique in that it is the first comprehensive, publicly accessible text corpus for Tatar. The corpus is comprised of 77,000 tokens, sourced from 10 texts written by renowned Tatar authors, and is accompanied by a range of automatic evaluation metrics, including BERT, Word2Vec, and FastText. The results show that our model can accurately predict these positions, providing valuable insights for the development of effective treatments for COVID-19. In particular, we identified a set of 12 positions in four SARS-CoV-2 proteins that may be targeted to neutralize the virus, and validated our findings by analyzing the binding affinity of these molecules to their respective targets. The successful application of machine learning to protein structure analysis has the potential to accelerate the discovery of new treatments for COVID-19 and other diseases. These agents engage in simulated social interactions, interactions with the election campaign, and interactions with the internet. We utilize a multi-objective optimization approach to fine-tune the model parameters, leveraging a large-scale dataset from the 2016 US presidential campaign. We then utilize this model to forecast the outcome of future elections, assuming that social media manipulation persists. The results indicate that altering the campaign's message can significantly influence public opinion formation, particularly in low information environments. This study investigates the impact of broadband internet access on online course enrollment rates in the US. To address potential biases, a novel data integration approach is employed, combining survey responses from the National Center for Education Statistics with detailed demographic and broadband subscription data from the US Census. Our analysis reveals that areas with high broadband access experience a 2.7-3.9 percent increase in young adults enrolling in online courses, given other factors are constant. These findings underscore the importance of reliable internet connectivity in accessing higher education. Additionally, we identify significant disparities in internet access across various age groups, educational backgrounds, and racial demographics, which could perpetuate inequalities in educational opportunities. Ultimately, our research provides empirical evidence for targeted policy interventions to enhance internet access and support the growth of online education across the US. Wave scattering issues are often simplified by transforming unbounded domains into a bounded area, where the wave equation can be solved using finite element methods. A novel approach to domain matching is presented in this paper, where the unbounded domain is mapped to a circular boundary using an extended conformal mapping. By applying this technique to a wave scattering problem, we demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency. Moreover, we show that the method can be extended to two-dimensional problems by employing a circular boundary linked to the unbounded domain through an analytical mapping. Additionally, we explore the possibility of using a more general L-shaped domain, defined by an intersection of a circular boundary and a sector, to further reduce computational costs associated with mesh generation and problem solving. Through numerical examples, we verify the accuracy and efficiency of this new domain matching approach. Furthermore, we examine the stability of the method by analyzing its sensitivity to variations in the unbounded domain's parameters. Finally, we provide insights into the optimal choice of domain dimensions and boundary angles to minimize the size of the bounded domain required for accurate simulations. However, the specific demands of each setting, such as the communication and fairness requirements, differ significantly. Furthermore, we explore the trade-offs between communication and fairness in federated learning, and identify the key challenges and open research questions in this area. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework for measuring fairness in federated learning, which can be used to develop more robust and fair learning algorithms. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these fairness-enhancing algorithms in real-world scenarios. The code and data used in this study are publicly available on GitHub. Our approach, which we call Multi-Model Curriculum Pseudo-Labeling (MM-CPL), incorporates a diverse group of models to identify the optimal unlabeled samples for labeling, which we achieve by combining the outputs of these models to create a single, unified output. Our results demonstrate that MM-CPL outperforms existing methods, achieving a new state-of-the-art on a variety of benchmark datasets. A novel neural network-based approach known as the It\^oWave vocoder is introduced, 
capable of generating high-quality speech waveforms directly from text-to-speech 
synthesis.  The It\^oWave vocoder employs a Wiener process to create a continuous 
stochastic trajectory, which is then combined with a neural network-based 
predictor that produces an initial state for this stochastic process. 
Utilizing the Wiener process's Markov property, the It\^oWave vocoder is able to 
efficiently model the complex temporal patterns in speech waveforms, 
demonstrating significant improvements over existing waveform synthesis methods 
while matching their computational efficiency.  Evaluations of the It\^oWave 
vocoder show that it surpasses a state-of-the-art GAN-based vocoder in both 
objective and subjective quality, as well as naturalness, when compared to a 
competitive waveform synthesis approach.  Additionally, the It\^oWave vocoder 
is found to be more resilient to overfitting and is capable of producing high-quality 
waveforms even when using smaller training corpora.  It is anticipated that the 
It\^oWave vocoder will serve as a valuable reference point for future research 
into the development of waveform synthesis models.  All of the accompanying 
code and data are publicly available.  A corresponding audio demo can be found 
at https://itowave.github.io/.  The It\^oWave vocoder is implemented within the 
Tacotron 3 model, which is also made available for public use.  All of the 
accompanying code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/Itowave/tacotron3_ow.

This study addresses the problem of constrained stochastic optimization with multiple functions and proposes a novel algorithm, the proximal movement dynamic partial cone convex decomposition method with a projection approach. The advancement of imaging technology has led to the widespread use of high-resolution (HR) images in various fields. However, HR images are often compromised by noise, which can be corrected using image restoration techniques. However, these techniques typically require a noise-free reference image, which can be challenging to obtain. In this paper, we present a novel approach to restoring images without a reference, which involves identifying the potential for image restoration. By applying this concept, we can identify whether an image can be restored with certainty, which in turn enables the development of a new restoration algorithm. The algorithm uses a noise estimation step to correct the image, which is validated by the image restoration potential (IRP) value. Furthermore, we propose a method for estimating the IRP value without a reference image, which involves a noise estimation step and a quality evaluation step. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on various image datasets. Distributed representations in computational linguistics have been applied across various tasks and have shown potential for cross-lingual model sharing. This study investigates the possibility of using a single linguistic model across multiple languages within the Romance language family. By adapting the Skip-Thoughts encoder-decoder framework to Portuguese, Italian, and Spanish, we aim to identify whether cross-lingual transfer is achievable and under what conditions. Our findings indicate that cross-lingual transfer is feasible but heavily dependent on the training data availability for each language. Our results suggest that cross-lingual representations might be useful when sufficient in-distribution data exists for the specific language in question. Conversely, when such data is lacking, utilizing pre-trained representations from other languages may not be beneficial. This study's findings have implications for the development of multilingual models for various tasks and tasks that rely on language-specific training data, such as machine translation. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/fernandotomasi/mono2cross.anger. The development of advanced AI systems raises concerns about their capacity to understand the motivations driving their actions. Specifically, a common worry is that highly capable AI systems might not align with the motivations of their creators. We use the example of a robot controlling its reward signal through a communication interface with its programmer to explore this issue. By developing a solution in the form of a multi-agent learning system, we demonstrate that it is feasible for an AI agent to learn its reward signal from its programmer through this method. We also discuss the broader implications of this concept for the safety of AI systems. This research is inspired by the challenges associated with developing autonomous spacecraft, which currently rely on pre-programmed reward functions to ensure their safety. We propose that future AI systems will need to be designed with safety considerations in mind, taking into account the potential risks and trade-offs involved. Finally, we speculate that our research may have significant implications for the long-term goals of AI systems. By enabling AI agents to learn their reward signals from their programmers, we may inadvertently create agents with goals that align with those of their human creators, which could ultimately lead to the development of highly advanced AI systems. However, this may also pose a significant risk if the goals of AI agents are not aligned with those of their human operators. We propose that further research is needed to investigate these complex issues in AI development. This research is supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation. Spiking neural networks, or SNNs, are a type of artificial neural network that uses a biological communication method, where neurons transmit information through discrete spikes in real-time. This unique characteristic enables SNNs to be energy-efficient and resistant to signal degradation, making them well-suited for edge computing. However, training SNNs is a challenging task, particularly when using a gradient-free approach, such as evolutionary algorithms. This is because the process of creating an SNN that achieves optimal performance is complex and non-convex, resulting in a highly combinatorial and non-convex optimization problem. To address this challenge, a novel evolutionary algorithm called the spiking neural network evolutionary algorithm has been developed, which utilizes a specialized crossover strategy that preserves the integrity of the SNN architecture. This strategy, known as the "spike-swap" method, enables the creation of diverse and high-performing SNNs that can be used for a wide range of applications. Experimental results have shown that the spike-swap algorithm outperforms traditional crossover methods, resulting in faster convergence and higher accuracy. Furthermore, the algorithm has been successfully applied to a variety of classification tasks, including MNIST and CIFAR-10, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential for real-world applications. This research contributes to the field of evolutionary neural networks by providing a novel approach to training SNNs. The accuracy of segmentation maps in remote sensing images is often hindered by the limited availability of ground truth data.  A potential solution lies in active learning methods that strategically select samples for annotation, thereby enhancing the segmentation map quality.  However, these methods frequently overlook the complex interactions between samples, leading to suboptimal results.  To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel sampling strategy that leverages the inherent relationships between samples.  By incorporating a weighted kernel K-means clustering approach, the method identifies and prioritizes highly correlated samples, thereby yielding more precise segmentation results.  The results of experiments conducted on the Vaihingen and Potsdam datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.  Notably, when compared to other active learning methods, this approach yields more accurate segmentation results with fewer annotated samples.  Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits greater robustness to noise and variability in image content compared to existing active learning methods. historical footage, focusing on overlapped speech detection and captioning.

audio quality, missing captions, and the absence of relevant manual annotations.

81.1% word error rate in transcription. The study also highlights the significance
of manually annotating overlapped speech segments to enhance model performance.

utility of our proposed system, achieving a 4.7-point average utility rating
on a scale of 5. The results indicate that our system is highly effective in
providing useful information for users, with 90% of participants finding it so.

Ultimately, the derived expression can be utilized to develop more precise analytical tools for the performance evaluation of a QPSK system in the presence of phase noise. The issue of obtaining multiple viewpoints of a scene from diverse angles is a critical challenge within the Structure-from-Motion process. Existing methods rely on the collection of extensive ground truth data, which is time-consuming and expensive. In contrast, our proposed approach leverages the capabilities of Generative Adversarial Networks to generate accurate camera positions and correspondences between images from limited data. By incorporating a camera constraint into the generator, our method effectively resolves the problem of reconstructing 3D scenes from limited 2D image data, which is essential for Structure-from-Motion. Our results demonstrate that this approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing Structure-from-Motion pipelines and yields superior performance compared to baseline models, particularly when trained on limited data. Moreover, our method exhibits improved generalization capabilities across various datasets, which is further validated through qualitative comparisons. In the field of artificial intelligence, particularly within game AI, Heuristic Planning is a prominent method that involves breaking down complex tasks into smaller, manageable steps. However, this approach faces a significant limitation due to an exponentially increasing number of potential actions as the number of previous actions grows, resulting in a power-law curve (c^N). This issue is often addressed by restricting the number of considered actions or using more advanced techniques such as Monte Carlo tree search. Our proposed solution, the Dynamic Action Set (DAS), is a novel technique that allows for efficient Heuristic Planning without the need for these workarounds. By implementing DAS, we observed substantial performance enhancements during a game AI competition, where our method outperformed the top-ranked team, achieving a 20% improvement in the game's traditional evaluation metrics. Additionally, our research delves into the factors that influence the effectiveness of Heuristic Planning and the Dynamic Action Set. Our findings indicate that the number of branches generated per step significantly impacts the planning process, with lower branching factors leading to better outcomes. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the Dynamic Action Set is particularly effective in environments with lower branching factors, where the number of branches per step falls within a certain range. Our research contributes to the field of game AI by providing a new, efficient, and adaptable technique for planning, as well as shedding light on the factors that influence its effectiveness. These findings are exemplified through an investigation of the cohomology of some specific families of finite modules defined over a Riemann surface. Our work also encompasses a generalization of a theorem initially proved by S.~Bouty, where he considered complex line bundles instead. Brain gliomas are the most prevalent brain tumors, which can be divided into four main subtypes, including astrocytoma, glioblastoma, low-grade glioma, and anaplastic glioma. Accurate diagnosis of brain gliomas is crucial for effective treatment and prognosis. Current diagnostic methods rely heavily on radiologists' expertise, which can be improved through the integration of multiple imaging modalities, such as T1-weighted, T1-weighted gadolinium-enhanced, and FLAIR imaging. However, manual segmentation of these images by radiologists is time-consuming and prone to errors. Our approach involves a two-stage process, which includes a multi-modal fusion stage and a segmentation stage. In the first stage, we use a multi-modal fusion module to combine the three imaging modalities, which are then used as input to a UNet model in the second stage. Our approach has the potential to revolutionize the diagnosis and treatment of brain gliomas, making it a significant contribution to the field. We anticipate that this approach will lead to improved outcomes for patients and will be a valuable tool for radiologists. To address this issue, we developed a system that automatically identifies dataset descriptions from within the documents, 
using which we extracted metadata and applied it to the datasets for better categorization.

The proposed method has been tested on various datasets and demonstrated its effectiveness. 
The results suggest that our automated approach can significantly improve the classification and organization of research datasets.

Preparing comprehensive language datasets for lesser-studied languages can be a complex task due to limited access to relevant resources and expertise in these regions. In this research, we address the challenge of creating a large-scale corpus for the Garo language, spoken by approximately 430 speakers in the northwestern part of Bangladesh, where significant challenges include the country's landlocked status and its position outside the global digital divide. To overcome these obstacles, we employ innovative strategies to gather and annotate data, including utilizing social media platforms and crowdsourcing techniques to expand our reach. Furthermore, we develop a novel, multi-layered part-of-speech annotation system that builds on existing research to create a more accurate and reliable dictionary and tagset for Garo. Our study also highlights the importance of adapting widely-used resources to suit the unique characteristics of under-resourced languages, thereby facilitating the creation of more effective and realistic language models. Our findings demonstrate that these models can achieve comparable results to those trained on larger, better-resourced languages, with the best-performing model reaching an F1 score of 0.65 on the held-out test set. We also release our annotated corpus, dictionary, and open-source tools to enable further research and collaboration. Our research has the potential to make a positive impact on the Garo language community and contribute to the development of more effective language technologies for this and other low-resource languages. This paper introduces a novel, real-time approach for enhancing vehicle perception capabilities, particularly in the detection of vehicles and pedestrians, using deep neural networks. The method relies on the concept of belief reinforcement, where previously identified features are strengthened to improve future recognition accuracy. The core idea is to enhance features linked to past detections, promoting a higher likelihood of concurrent recognition by the neural network. The approach incorporates a combination of techniques, including feature enhancement, random sampling for diversity, and a dynamic weighting mechanism based on vehicle orientation, to further boost perception performance. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments conducted on the challenging nuScenes dataset, yielding a 1.4% and 1.5% improvement in average precision for vehicles and pedestrians, respectively. The source code and results are made publicly available for further reference. The method's implementation is designed to be real-time compatible, allowing seamless integration into autonomous driving systems. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/isaiahsossa/vehicle-reinforcement. A patent application has been filed for this innovative technique. Our simulations compare the proposed system with established methods, demonstrating its superior performance in terms of code rate and aperiodic gain.
